chapter_theme: Paripadal 11, to the Vaigai: the flood dated by the stars, the flowers it carries to the ford, a plea that the river go gently, the town's water-sport drawn as war, the maidens' Thai bath under the brahmins' rite, a youth swept off by the current as a girl takes his heart, the bathers' prayers for lasting love, and a close that names the song a kaikkilai.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of the Vaigai flood told as praise of the river, under paadaan

paripadal:11:1-15.reading: The poet fixes the hour of the flood by the sky: with the moon among the twenty-seven stars that the fire-star, the matted one and the elephant head, Venus come to the Bull, the earth's son to the Ram, Mercury joined to the Twins, the fire high at dawn, the other planets at their stations by the Bow and Capricorn, the serpent swiftly hiding the moon, and the star of the sage of Pothiyil reaching the Twins, so that rain might come to meet the blazing summer; and by this course the rain falls low on the lofty Sahya and the Vaigai's flood comes crowding down.
paripadal:11:1-15.nuance: The song opens not with a god but with a dated sky: the river's coming is placed inside the order of stars and planets, as if the flood were a festival with its own horoscope. Which planet each name in lines 7 to 9 stands for (அந்தணன், பங்கு, இறை யமன்) is a reading, not a certainty, and the eclipse of line 9 (பாம்பு ... மதியம் மறைய) may be a fixed event or a figure.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the river's ford by what its flood brings, under paadaan

paripadal:11:16-30.reading: The flood brings down the punnai of the hills and the surapunnai of the banks, rows of champak hummed over by bees, the house mango, the vaal veeram, the branching vengai, the wide-opened kaanthal, thondri blooming like fire and bright blue lilies opened by the wind, choking the falls of the bamboo groves and driving them on its leaping waves, so that the poet asks whether to call the great Thirumarudam ford a ford of flowers cut by the reapers, a woman's garment with flowers for its upper cloth, foam for its pearl-hung breast and fragrant paste for its sandal, or the throat of a drinker gulping toddy.
paripadal:11:16-30.nuance: The three 'shall I call it' questions (என்கோ, lines 25 to 29) give the same ford three bodies: worked land, a dressed woman and a drunk man, so the flood is at once harvest, ornament and intoxication. ஆய் கோல் வயவர் (lines 24, 25) may be reapers or warriors; the sense of the first figure is not secure. The flowers are mostly of the hill, carried down into the town's ford.

comparisons.tenor: the ford covered with flowers, foam and fragrant paste

thinai_evidence.note: address and counsel to the river, under paadaan

paripadal:11:31-45.reading: Like the waxing fortnight of the full moon the flood grows day by day, touches the slopes of the thick hills and spreads over the land as moonlight spreads, so that the world yields its fruit; then, as the moon's fullness wastes in the fortnight when the gods take their food from it, the flow shrinks, and who notices the days run down like the moon of the dark new-moon after its fullness? So the poet asks the jewelled Vaigai, who came from afar riding over stones, to go gently that her plenty may last its full term, and tells her that, as peacock-like women who joined young men in secret leave stealth and take up chastity, for her to leave the great mountain and go alone to a house would be a shame.
paripadal:11:31-45.nuance: The river is spoken to as a bride: the move from களவு to கற்பு (line 42) is the passage she is making from the hill to the plain, and the poet's counsel is that she not go alone, that is, that her flood go with its full train. The word இளிவரல் (line 44) is a judgment of shame, not the meyppadu of that name, whose causes are age and illness. The run of lines 41 to 44 is compressed and its exact construction is a reading.

comparisons.tenor: the flood growing day by day
the water spreading over the land
the women who pass from secret love to marriage

comparisons.vehicle: காமம் கள விட்டு, கைகொள் கற்பு உற்றென
comparisons.tenor: the river leaving the mountain for the plain

thinai_evidence.note: lovers' water-sport in the town's river, the play of the cultivated tract

paripadal:11:46-61.reading: As when kinsmen fall on a youth in mid-road as he carries off with his band a girl whose long wide eyes outrun their corners, the flood strikes warlike Madurai and its water is fit for play: the river's array is men brandishing white swords and lifting gleaming lances, men mounting strong bannered chariots as the drivers take the goad, men who ride bird-swift horses and gold-trapped elephants again and again through the flood, men who throw balls hiding coloured water at those who chase with poles, and men who squirt water from rough horns at those who whirl fragrant garlands, so that, when one tells the fearsome sight of the well-garlanded women sporting with their lovers, the Vaigai's waters are every day like a field of battle.
paripadal:11:46-61.nuance: The water-sport is drawn entirely in the terms of war (swords, lances, chariots, horses, elephants, a battlefield), and the opening simile is itself an elopement broken by the girl's kin: the flood that breaks on the town is the pursuing family, and the town is the couple. Lines 54 to 57 (கழித் துரப்போரை, வட்டு, மருப்பின் நீர் எக்குவோரும்) name games whose exact form is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: couples drinking and embracing on the river, the union of the town's lovers

paripadal:11:62-73.reading: Men with chests broad as hills, wearing cool garlands thick with fragrant water-flowers, go with women of fine jewels and worked gold garlands; they drink the honeyed wine, the elation spreads, and the townsmen press close to embrace; each draws the other's beauty in through the eyes, ears stirred by well-made song, on boats that ride like the bright cars of those who dwell above, a custom with nothing hidden; and so, O Vaigai, your turbid summer water and its clearing are not like the rains.
paripadal:11:62-73.nuance: The unit is one long run of attributes (lines 62 to 65 heap seven qualifiers on the women's garlands) closed by a plain address to the river. கரவா வழக்கிற்று (line 71), 'a custom that does not hide', makes the lovers' play public, the opposite of the secrecy of களவு in the earlier unit. Lines 66, 67 and 72, 73 are obscure in construction.

thinai_evidence.note: the river's rite and offering, praise of the river under paadaan

paripadal:11:74-92.reading: When the thundering rain clouds have gone and the cold dewy shivering season comes, after the heavy rains when the sun does not scorch, on the Aathirai of the full moon the learned brahmins begin the festival and thread-wearing brahmins receive the golden vessels; praying that the wide earth not be scorched, the maidens of fine bangles in the ambaa bath, shown the order of the rite by the elder women of the ford, bathe at the cold dawn, and as the wind blows over the sandy stream they dry their wet clothes at the leaning flame the vedic priests tend; so, O Vaigai, your offering was fitting. Then the poet asks the river: is it through hard penance done before, beside the fire, that these girls bathe in the Thai water standing near their mothers, while the young poets rise against one another in their contests?
paripadal:11:74-92.nuance: The bath is for the land, not (as later tradition has it) for a husband: the girls' stated prayer is வெம்பாதாக, வியல் நில வரைப்பு (line 80). Brahmin priests, elder women and mothers frame the maidens' rite, so the unmarried girls' bathing is a public act under guardians. Lines 88 and 89 (மையாடல் ஆடல் மழ புலவர் மாறு எழுந்து, பொய் ஆடல்) are obscure; the contest of the young poets is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a first look between a girl and a youth that the flood and her mother cut off before any union, the love the song itself calls kaikkilai

paripadal:11:93-114.reading: On the bank the girls adorn one another in rivalry: one, her shoulders surpassing the bamboo, sets tender asoka shoots and a blue lily at her ears, so that it is said she has made herself four eyes; another answers with a tilaka like a forehead eye, taking the look of Kotravai; one, seeing a girl in coral bangles, puts on green lily stalks; and against one who strings a kallakaaram wreath another, as if saying 'stop!', winds neythal round a jasmine garland; then in the leaping Vaigai a youth loses hold of his float the moment he sees one of them, the strong current takes his hand, she takes his heart and the long raft is swept off, his eyes stay where she stands while the water carries him where it will, she leaves her companions to follow him, and her mother, not knowing why, holds her back crying 'don't go alone, keep with your group', as the new flood from far away comes striking down.
paripadal:11:93-114.nuance: Three pulls in one line (கை வாங்க, நெஞ்சம் அவள் வாங்க, புணை வாங்க, lines 107, 108): the river, the girl and the float each take something from him, so the flood that carries the body is the outward form of the look that carries the heart. The mother's தனிச் சேறல் (line 112) repeats the poet's word to the river in line 44: the girl and the river are warned in the same phrase. நில்லிகா and மல்லிகா (lines 104, 105) are a pun.

comparisons.tenor: the blue lilies set at her ears
the rival girl winding neythal round jasmine

thinai_evidence.note: the bathers' praise of and petitions to the Thai water, under paadaan, carrying love's matter

paripadal:11:115-132.reading: Some say 'you are worthy, Thai water, your colour has cleared'; some 'we pray that we may win the honour of embracing lovers whose arms never leave our necks'; some 'may those we love not leave us lonely as the bee leaves a fallen flower, but be our safe keeping'; some 'never saying old man and old woman, for seven births may our rich kin last, bearing children'; and the onlookers call out: this beauty is a goddess that strikes whoever sees her, her eyes are Kaaman's treasury and army; hear the swarm of bees that will not leave though the women with oiled lily garlands drive them off, holding a tune as on a lute; hear the bright paalai melody of the bees attending their kin; see the cool thumbis dancing to the beat; see the one thumbi in burning anger that dives first at the girl who crushed the flower it loved.
paripadal:11:115-132.nuance: The four prayers rise in scope: a clear river, a lover's embrace, a lover who will not leave, and a household that lasts seven births without growing old. The angry thumbi of lines 130 to 132 guards the flower it loves against the girl who crushed it; it could be read as a figure for the lover's jealousy, but no situation in the unit is anchored to it, so it is left as scene. The music terms of lines 126 to 129 are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing praise and prayer to the river, under paadaan

paripadal:11:133-140.reading: So the poet closes: through penance done before, we have come together this time in your Thai bathing of such a kind, this sweet, finely wrought paripadal song of the kaikkilai love of a maiden of shining jewels and fragrant brow whose maidenhood has not ripened; may we come together again at the next time too, O fragrant-watered Vaigai, fulness worth desiring.
paripadal:11:133-140.nuance: The song names its own genre and theme in lines 136 and 137: கைக்கிளைக் காம(ம்) of a maiden whose maidenhood has not ripened, which fits the broken-off look of lines 93 to 114. இம் முறை ... மறு முறை (lines 138, 139) can be this festival and the next, or this birth and the next; the merit of earlier penance (முன் முறை செய் தவம்) favours the larger reading but does not fix it.

links.note: Paripadal 11.37-38 asks who notices the days run down (நாள் குறைபடுதல் காணுநர் யாரே) as the flood wanes like the moon; Kural 334 says the day is a saw cutting life, for those who can perceive it (உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்).
links.teaches: Both turn on the same observation, that daily loss goes unseen, but the Paripadal draws from it a request to the river to slow down and keep its plenty, while the Kural draws a warning to the perceptive; the image of unnoticed waning could serve plenty as well as renunciation.

links.note: Paripadal 11.62-71 praises the Vaigai water-sport of men with gold-garlanded women as an open custom (கரவா வழக்கிற்று); in Akananuru 296 the friend refuses a husband who bathed in the great Vaigai with another woman and says it is already common talk.
links.teaches: The same Madurai river festival that the devotional song celebrates as a public glory with nothing hidden is, seen from the wife's door, the proof and occasion of a husband's straying, so the openness the Paripadal praises is exactly what feeds the alar of the marutham quarrel.

links.note: Natrinai 80 names in one line a girl who bathes in the cold pond of the month of Thai with her jewelled companions (தைஇத் திங்கள் தண் கயம் படியும்); Paripadal 11.74-92 sets out the rite itself: Aathirai, the brahmins, the elder women of the ford, the dawn bath and the fire.
links.teaches: The akam poem's passing mention of a Thai bath points to a guarded public rite with priests, elder women and mothers, so the girl a lover sees there is seen at a sanctioned gathering of maidens, which is why such a meeting could happen and why shyness must restrain her.

links.note: In Paripadal 11.80 unmarried girls bathe under the brahmins' fire rite praying 'may the wide land not be scorched'; Kural 55 says it rains at the word of the wife who does not worship a god but worships her husband. On the plain reading these name incompatible sources of the rain women can bring: public worship by maidens, or a wife's devotion that sets worship of a god aside.
links.teaches: Held together, the pair shows two rival accounts of women's power over the rain, the festival rite of the unmarried at the river and the wife's domestic devotion, and the Kural's தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் reads as a choice of the second over the first.

links.note: Paripadal 11.106-110 tells literally of a youth whom the Vaigai's current carries off while a girl takes his heart (கடும் புனல் கை வாங்க, நெஞ்சம் அவள் வாங்க); in Kalittokai 98 a husband swears he was delayed bathing in the Vaigai's new flood, and his wife answers that people saw the new flood drag him off, a flood that was a woman.
links.teaches: The wife's figure of the woman as a flood that carried him off is the Paripadal's festival event turned into an accusation, so the river festival was both the occasion of a man being swept away by a look and the stock excuse for it, and the Kalittokai's irony depends on the audience knowing the Paripadal scene.

links.note: Paripadal 11.120-121 has the bathing women ask that for seven births, without growing old, their rich kin last and bear children; in Kuruntokai 49 a wife asks her husband that even when this birth gives way to the next he be her husband and she the one close to his heart.
links.teaches: What the Kuruntokai wife says privately to one man, the Paripadal's women ask together of the river at a public festival, so the wish to keep the same spouse beyond this birth was a recognised petition of the Thai rite, not only one woman's vow of love.

links.note: Paripadal 11.122-123 has onlookers call a girl a striking goddess (தாக்கு அணங்கு) whose eyes are Kaaman's army (காமன் படை); Kural 1082 has the man say that her returning his look is a striking goddess come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்ன).
links.teaches: The rare compound and the army come together in both, so the Kural's lover is speaking a festival idiom: what the Paripadal's crowd shouts as a warning to all who see the girl, the Kural turns into one man's private experience of a single returned glance.

source_issues: Paripadal 11: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai. The song names its own theme in line 136 (கைக்கிளைக் காம).
Paripadal 11 line 59: உருகெமு is a misprint for உருகெழு (as in line 4).
Paripadal 11 line 113: எந்று is a misprint for என்று.
Paripadal 11 lines 100 and 127: ஒர் and ஒர்மின் for ஓர் and ஓர்மின் (lost vowel length).

Paripadal 11 lines 1, 51, 64 and 137: flagged as places where a line was taken for a modern heading and dropped; the text as printed reads continuously at each, but this was not verified against another edition.
Paripadal 11 lines 32-34, 50-53 and 56-60 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags). Line 47: lost vowel sign restored in படையொடும் by rule (flag).
